15u4remc1qs: An antivirus assumes that everything runs except what it recognizes as malicious. Application control reverses the logic: **code runs only if the policy allows it**. It covers executables, libraries, MSI installers, scripts and even interactive PowerShell sessions. It does not replace the antivirus: it complements it. Windows offers two technologies. **App Control for Business** (formerly WDAC) is designed as a security feature and serves as the reference; **AppLocker** is a legacy technology that is still supported, which now receives only security fixes. Microsoft's recommendation: favor App Control for Business, except for a specific need (per-user rules, for example) that only AppLocker fills.
60rvd9r5x4: In Endpoint security > App Control for Business, two formats: **XML** (you supply the full policy) or **built-in controls** (approve what a managed installer installs, trust Windows components and Store applications). An empty "XML" policy acts as Not configured. Without an allow rule, anything not explicitly permitted is blocked, except in **audit mode** where everything runs and the details are logged locally. Intune relies on the ApplicationControl CSP. A base policy can be extended with **supplemental policies** (written in XML). Several base and supplemental policies can coexist on a device. The older "Application Control" instances in the attack surface reduction profiles will be retired: do not use them for a new project.

Applications deployed **before** the designation are not tagged: deploy in audit to spot what is missing, then create supplemental policies. nys4rd0n52: Defender for Endpoint Device Control restricts access to **Windows portable devices**, **removable media**, **CD/DVDs** and **printers**. On Windows, "removable media" does not mean "any USB device": to be in scope, the device **must create a disk** (for example E:). A USB mouse or keyboard is not concerned. To block other classes, you need Windows **device installation restrictions** (by device ID, instance ID or setup class); these restrictions block everything that appears in Device Manager, including essential devices, so target them with care. The CSP setting that denies write access to removable disks also exists as a simpler measure. Another separate route: endpoint DLP (module 10) monitors actions on sensitive content but is not an access control for media.
1axotkbfh6h: A **policy** defines access for a set of devices. A **rule** lists included groups and excluded groups: it applies if the device is in *all* the included groups and in *none* of the excluded groups. The rule's **entries** specify the action (allow, deny, audit), the notification options and the access mask (read, write, execute, print), optionally limited to a user (Entra object ID or SID) or to a device group. If no rule or entry matches, the **default enforcement** decides.
mvv8glhx12: By default, Device Control is disabled and everything is allowed. Once enabled, it targets all device types, with a default enforcement that can be switched from Allow to Deny. Central Intune trap: **rule order is not preserved**. Write Allow and Deny rules that **do not overlap**, explicitly excluding the groups out of scope. Another trap: **you cannot change the default enforcement in the Intune graphical interface**; if you set it to Deny by another route (custom OMA-URI profile: DeviceControlEnabled, DefaultEnforcement = 2, SecuredDevicesConfiguration = RemovableMediaDevices) and then create an Allow rule for certain devices, all the others are blocked. If you configure only audit rules, the permissions come from the default enforcement: always add an Allow or Deny rule along with the audit.

The events appear in Advanced Hunting and in the Device Control report.

xb2s7ai14: An update ring applies the Windows Update client settings to a group of devices. Three levers not to be confused. The **deferral** delays the offer of an update for a number of days after its release: it is the observation time. The **deadline** sets the number of days, after the offer, before forced installation; the catalog accepts 2 to 30 days for quality and feature updates. The **grace period** sets the minimum number of days after the deadline before the automatic restart (0 to 7 days). The deferral decides *when to offer*, the deadline *when to force*, the grace *when to restart*. A device that has not restarted is not patched, even if the update is installed.
264u22e6woo: The classic approach uses **Test**, **Pilot**, **Fast**, **Broad** and **Critical devices** groups. The first receive the update early (short deferral, short deadline) and serve as detectors; the last receive it after observation. Example of a Microsoft educational template: quality deferral of 7 days, quality deadline of 3 days, grace of 2 days, automatic restart before the deadline enabled. For critical devices, disable the automatic restart before the deadline and schedule a window. The values are starting points, not standards: the right value depends on the risk of regression and the risk of exposure.

10oba9jagth: Windows Update and the policies in this module concern Windows, quality and feature updates, certain drivers and the supported .NET Framework. **Third-party applications** (browsers, PDF readers, VPN clients, Java runtimes) are a frequent operational blind spot. Microsoft offers **Enterprise App Management**: a catalog of prepared Win32 applications, Microsoft and non-Microsoft, hosted by Microsoft. **Nature: add-on feature under additional license**: it requires a subscription on top of Intune Plan 1 or 2, sold alone or in the Intune suite. Windows only.
kz3i86l71b: The catalog does not verify your application licenses; you remain responsible for purchasing and distributing licenses. Application updates are generally available within 24 hours after automated validation, and up to seven days if a manual test is required: it is not an instant fix. Applications that update themselves are considered installed from a minimum version and update according to the vendor; the network must allow the vendor's updates. Automatic update applies only to catalog applications with a **Required** assignment. It offers **neither rollback nor automatic corrective uninstall**, **nor phased deployment rings**. If Microsoft withdraws a malicious version, you must yourself identify the affected devices and fix them; catalog data is cached for up to an hour, so an hour of exposure is possible after a revocation. If you prefer to review each update, use guided supersedence. An application removed from the catalog remains functional on the devices where it is deployed but can no longer be newly deployed.
